Dermatology · published research

Atopic dermatitis

A sham-controlled trial found short-term changes in itch and some patient-rated measures, but not clear improvement in clinician-rated severity. The human evidence does not establish lasting disease control.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A sham-controlled trial found short-term changes in itch and some patient-rated measures, but not clear improvement in clinician-rated severity. The human evidence does not establish lasting disease control.

Summary of the Evidence

Nine publications are assigned to atopic dermatitis: two human studies, six mouse studies, and one canine study. The human evidence includes an 87-participant randomized sham-controlled trial and an older retrospective series of 81 patients. No standalone in-vitro study is listed. The animal experiments use different strains, light protocols, and co-interventions, so their results do not represent one uniform treatment.

Human and clinical evidence

In the AD-Blue trial, 87 participants received full-body blue-light exposure at 415 nm or 450 nm, or sham treatment, for eight weeks, with four weeks of follow-up. The report found changes in some symptom-oriented measures, including itch with the 450 nm protocol and patient-oriented SCORAD with 415 nm, but did not find significant differences in the principal clinician-rated EASI, SCORAD, or IGA outcomes versus sham. The study reported no safety signal during its follow-up (Buhl et al. 2023). An older uncontrolled series using near-infrared light reported reduced itch or eruptions in many participants, but without a comparator it cannot distinguish treatment effects from concurrent care or changes over time.

Animal evidence

Most of the six mouse studies report changes in dermatitis scores, immunoglobulin E, inflammatory cytokines, epidermal thickness, or mast-cell infiltration. Some protocols combine light with curcumin, tacrolimus, or other interventions, and responses vary by model. The single canine study of pedal pruritus did not report a clear benefit.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell or tissue study was identified in this category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The controlled human study compared 415 nm and 450 nm, both in the visible blue region, using full-body exposure over eight weeks. The older series used 830 nm near-infrared light, but its treatment parameters and design are less complete. These wavelengths, exposure areas, and outcomes are not directly interchangeable. No human dose-finding comparison establishes an optimal protocol, and short-term symptom changes should not be taken as durable disease control.

Interpretation

The clinical evidence separates itch or patient-rated changes from clinician-rated dermatitis severity: the blinded trial found some symptom differences but no clear change in its main clinical severity measures. The older series cannot resolve that distinction. Animal findings help generate questions but do not estimate treatment effects in people.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term itch reduction with selected blue-light protocols Very low for clinician-rated severity or sustained disease control
Publications and records9 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One sham-controlled trial found changes in some itch and patient-rated measures, while its main clinician-rated severity outcomes did not significantly differ from sham. An older uncontrolled series also reported symptom changes, and animal work is mixed. A larger blinded trial using common severity measures and longer follow-up would be needed to assess disease control.
